title: Should Christians Become Influencers? The Question Isn’t Whether People See You—It’s Who They See Through You
paragraphs: Should Christians Become Influencers? The Question Isn’t Whether People See You—It’s Who They See Through You

The internet tells you to build a name, grow an audience, protect your image, and make people remember you. Jesus calls you to something far more dangerous: become visible enough for people to see the light—and surrendered enough that they forget you and remember Him.
There is a strange moment that happens when a post begins to take off.
The notifications keep coming.
Someone shared it.
Someone tagged a friend.
Ten comments become a hundred. A hundred followers become a thousand. Suddenly people are listening to what you say.
And somewhere between the first notification and the thousandth follower, a question begins whispering inside the heart:
What if I could become somebody?
That question isn't automatically sinful.
But it can become spiritually dangerous very quickly.
Because there is another question hiding beneath it.
Do I want people to encounter Jesus…or do I secretly need them to notice me?
That is where the conversation about Christian influencers must begin.
Not with algorithms.
Not with follower counts.
Not with whether Christians should use Facebook, YouTube, TikTok, Instagram, podcasts, books, livestreams, or whatever platform comes next.
The issue is the heart.
And Scripture refuses to let us hide from it.
Jesus looked at His disciples and said something astonishing:
“Ὑμεῖς ἐστε τὸ φῶς τοῦ κόσμου.”
Hymeis este to phōs tou kosmou.
“You are the light of the world.” — Matthew 5:14.
Notice what Jesus did not say.
He did not tell His followers to become invisible.
He did not command them to withdraw from every public square.

In the verses that follow, He speaks about a city that cannot be hidden and a lamp that is not placed under a basket. Then comes the purpose: people are to see the believers' good works and glorify their Father in heaven.
There is visibility in Christianity.
There is public witness.
There is influence.
But there is a massive difference between being seen so God is glorified and using God so we can be seen.
And that difference may be one of the most important spiritual battles facing Christians in the age of social media.
Because only a chapter later, Jesus gives what initially sounds like the opposite warning.
He warns His disciples not to practice righteousness before people in order to be seen by them. — Matthew 6:1.
Read those truths together.
Matthew 5: let them see.
Matthew 6: don't do it to be seen.
That is not a contradiction.
That is heart surgery.
Jesus is exposing the motive.
The same outward action can come from radically different hearts.
One person can speak publicly about Christ because they desperately want Christ known.
Another can speak publicly about Christ because they desperately want themselves known.
Sometimes nobody watching can tell the difference.
Sometimes even the person posting cannot tell anymore.
That is why the most dangerous thing about Christian influence may not be becoming famous.
It may be becoming addicted to being noticed while convincing yourself that everything is “for God's glory.”
That sentence should make every Christian creator uncomfortable.
Including us.
Especially us.
Because the moment ministry becomes immune to self-examination, ministry becomes vulnerable to self-worship.
Paul gives perhaps the clearest biblical sentence for anyone who wants influence in the name of Jesus:
“For we preach not ourselves, but Christ Jesus the Lord; and ourselves your servants for Jesus' sake.” — 2 Corinthians 4:5, KJV.
The heart of the sentence is devastatingly simple.
Not ourselves. Christ Jesus as Lord.

The Greek behind Paul's language makes the contrast unmistakable. The apostolic proclamation is not centered upon the messengers themselves; Christ Jesus is proclaimed as Lord, while the messengers take the posture of servants. That is also how major English translations consistently render the verse.
There is the biblical theology of Christian influence.
You may have a platform.
You may have reach.
You may have a microphone.
You may have a million followers.
But the microphone is not a throne.
The platform is not an altar to your personality.
And followers are not disciples who belong to you.
Jesus is Lord.
You are a servant.
That changes everything.
So, should Christians become influencers?
Perhaps we need to stop asking whether Christians should become “influencers” and start asking whether Christians are willing to become faithful witnesses who happen to have influence.
Because influence itself is morally neutral.
A mother influences her children.
A pastor influences a congregation.
A teacher influences students.
A teenager influences friends.
A businessman influences employees.
A woman sharing what Christ carried her through may influence someone she will never meet.
A man opening Scripture on camera from his bedroom may reach a lonely believer thousands of miles away.
The question is not whether you influence people.
You already do.
The question is:
Where are you influencing them to go?
Toward admiration of you?
Toward envy of your life?
Toward dependency on your personality?
Toward endless controversy?
Toward consumerism disguised as Christianity?
Or toward repentance, grace, truth, holiness, forgiveness, Scripture, the cross, the empty tomb, and Jesus Christ?
Because eventually every platform becomes a signpost.
And every signpost points somewhere.
Imagine standing before Christ one day and discovering that thousands knew your face but barely knew His Word.
Imagine people remembering your catchphrases but not His commands.
Imagine building an audience around Christianity while quietly building your identity around applause.
Imagine defending biblical truth publicly while neglecting prayer privately.
Imagine gaining followers while losing tenderness toward God.
Imagine becoming known for Jesus while slowly forgetting how to sit alone with Jesus when nobody is watching.
That is the scandal hiding beneath Christian celebrity.
And none of us should assume we are above it.
James gives another sobering warning:
“Not many of you should become teachers, my brothers, for you know that we who teach will be judged with greater strictness.” — James 3:1.
Influence increases responsibility.
More reach does not simply mean more opportunity.
It means more accountability.
Every person teaching Scripture publicly should feel some weight when pressing “Post.”
Is this true?
Did Scripture actually say this?
Am I forcing the Bible to support something I already wanted to say?
Am I stirring fear because fear gets engagement?
Am I manufacturing outrage because outrage gets shares?
Am I turning someone's pain into content?
Am I making promises God never made?
Am I preaching Christ—or performing Christianity?
Those questions matter because human souls are not analytics.
A view count has a person behind it.
A comment has a story behind it.
A share may land on the screen of someone sitting alone at 2:13 in the morning wondering whether God could possibly forgive what they have done.
That person does not need a Christian celebrity.
They need Christ.
They need to know that sin is real, judgment is real, repentance matters—and grace is more glorious than the scandal they thought disqualified them forever.
They need to know there is a Savior who did not merely give motivational advice from heaven.
He came.
He entered our broken world.
He touched people respectable religion avoided.
He confronted hypocrisy.
He called sinners to repentance.
He carried the cross.
He shed His blood.
He died.
He was buried.
And He rose.
The Gospel is not “believe in yourself.”
The Gospel is that sinful human beings can be reconciled to a holy God through Jesus Christ.
That is why Christian influence must ultimately become smaller at the foot of the cross.
Because the cross destroys our obsession with image.
At Calvary, there are no impressive influencers.
There are sinners who need mercy.
There are no follower counts impressive enough to purchase forgiveness.
There are no verified badges that open heaven.
There are no algorithms that can resurrect a dead heart.
There is Christ.
Crucified.
Risen.
Lord.
And grace.
This is where something beautiful can happen to the Christian who has been chasing recognition.
Jesus does not merely expose our vanity to humiliate us.
He calls us out of slavery to it.
Maybe you started posting because you loved Jesus.
Then somewhere along the way, numbers began determining your mood.
A successful post made you feel valuable.
A failed post made you question yourself.
Someone else's growth made you jealous.
Someone else's ministry began feeling like competition.
You refreshed the analytics again.
And again.
And again.
You told yourself you were checking “the reach.”
But underneath it, perhaps you were checking whether you still mattered.
Jesus offers something better.
Your identity was never supposed to live inside a dashboard.
You were not redeemed by engagement.
You were redeemed by Christ.
You do not need strangers to validate what the cross has already declared about the astonishing mercy of God toward those who belong to Jesus.
That freedom changes how you influence.
Now you can tell the truth even when truth performs badly.
You can refuse clickbait that distorts Scripture.
You can admit when you were wrong.
You can delete something misleading.
You can refuse to exploit tragedy.
You can celebrate another ministry's fruit without secretly resenting it.
You can serve people who can do absolutely nothing for your platform.
You can disappear for prayer without panicking that the algorithm will forget you.
You can lose followers for refusing to compromise.
You can become less impressive and more faithful.
You can mean it when you say:
If they remember anything, let them remember Jesus.
That is Christian influence redeemed.
Not celebrity baptized in religious vocabulary.
Not personal branding with Bible verses sprinkled over it.
Not turning the Gospel into a ladder toward fame.
It is stewardship.
It is carrying light into dark places while remembering that you are not the source of the light.
It is standing where people can see you while continually pointing beyond yourself.
And perhaps that is why John the Baptist remains such a powerful picture for anyone with an audience.
People were coming to him.
People were listening.
His ministry had attention.
Yet when Christ came into view, John's instinct was not to protect his market share.
“He must increase, but I must decrease.” — John 3:30.
What a terrifying prayer for an influencer.
Jesus, increase even if I decrease.
Could you pray it?
Jesus, increase even if people stop mentioning my name.
Jesus, increase even if someone else gets the opportunity.
Jesus, increase even if my numbers fall because I refuse to compromise.
Jesus, increase even if the truth costs me popularity.
Jesus, increase even if everything I built becomes merely a road someone traveled to find You.
That is surrender.
And surrender is where influence becomes ministry.
This is also why supporting Christian work must never be presented as purchasing God's favor.
Grace cannot be purchased.
The Gospel cannot be bought.
Christ has already paid the price sinners could never pay.
But grace creates generosity.

When believers freely support faithful Gospel work, they can help Scripture-centered teaching travel farther, resources reach more people, and ministry continue. Paul himself describes believers participating in Gospel ministry through giving and partnership, while the New Testament repeatedly insists that giving must not be coerced.
But there is something you can do without spending anything.
Not because sharing a post earns glory for God automatically. It doesn't.
Someone you know may be building an image while their soul is starving.
Someone may be comparing their tiny ministry with somebody else's enormous platform.
Someone may believe they are useless because only twenty people listen to them.
Someone may secretly be addicted to applause.
Someone may have walked away from Christianity after watching Christian personalities fall.
Someone may need to discover that Christianity was never ultimately about the personality holding the microphone.
It was always about Jesus.
If sharing this can put that truth in front of one person who needs it, then use your influence for that.
If this exposed something uncomfortable in you, don't manufacture a polished spiritual answer.
Your honesty may give another believer permission to stop pretending.
Because success has a strange way of making yesterday's convictions easy to forget.
Come back when the numbers start climbing.
Come back when they collapse.
Come back when someone praises you.
Come back when someone criticizes you.
Come back when another Christian passes you.
Come back when you're tempted to compromise truth for reach.
And remember:
The goal was never to make your name impossible to ignore. The goal was to live so faithfully that your life makes Jesus harder to ignore.
Maybe Christians should become influencers.
But only if we are willing to redefine influence at the cross.
Influence is not how many people know your name.
It is what happens in someone's life because you were faithful with what God placed in your hands.
Maybe your audience is five people.
Love them.
Maybe it is fifty.
Serve them.
Maybe it is fifty thousand.
Tremble a little.
Stay humble.
Stay teachable.
Stay accountable.
Open your Bible more than you open your analytics.
Pray when nobody can photograph it.
Repent when nobody can monetize it.
Tell the truth when lies would travel faster.
Refuse to turn wounds into branding.
Never confuse followers with disciples.
Never confuse visibility with anointing.
Never confuse virality with faithfulness.
And never forget that the greatest thing your platform can ever accomplish is not making people say,
“What an incredible Christian.”
It is making someone whisper,
“I need Jesus.”
Because one day the screen will go dark.
The notifications will stop.
The audience will move on.
Your name will eventually disappear from timelines.
But Christ will still be King.
So build accordingly.
Speak accordingly.
Post accordingly.
Live accordingly.
And if God gives you influence, hold it with an open hand.
Because perhaps the holiest thing an influencer can finally become is a signpost nobody worships, pointing toward a Savior nobody can afford to miss.
Let your name become smaller if necessary. Let your reach become smaller if necessary. But never make Jesus smaller so your platform can become bigger.
